message.content:
The 19th‑century sculpture that most people think of when they hear “famous” is **Auguste Rodin’s *The Kiss* (1889)**. ### Why *The Kiss* stands out | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Artist** | Auguste Rodin (France) | | **Date** | 1889 (first cast) | | **Style** | Realist/Impressionist, early modernism | | **Subject** | A passionate embrace between two lovers, rendered with dramatic, almost raw flesh and movement | | **Impact** | • One of the first sculptures to capture a moment of intense emotion rather than a static pose.
• Influenced generations of sculptors and painters.
• Became a symbol of romantic love and artistic freedom. | | **Legacy** | • Widely reproduced in bronze, marble, and other media.
• Displayed in major museums worldwide (e.g., Musée Rodin, Paris; National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.).
• Continues to be referenced in popular culture, advertising, and academic discussions. | ### Other contenders | Sculpture | Artist | Year | Why it matters | |-----------|--------|------|----------------| | **The Gates of Hell** | Rodin | 1880–1917 (unfinished) | Massive, complex work that pushed the limits of bronze casting and narrative sculpture. | | **The Statue of Liberty** | Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi | 1886 | Iconic national monument, a collaboration between sculpture and engineering. | | **The Thinker** | Rodin | 1902 (late 19th‑early 20th) | Though technically from the early 20th century, it became the quintessential symbol of intellectual contemplation. | ### Bottom line While several 19th‑century works have left an indelible mark, Rodin’s *The Kiss* is often regarded as the most famous because it captured a universal human emotion in a way that was both innovative and widely accessible. Its influence on modern sculpture and its enduring presence in museums and popular culture make it the standout piece of that era.
